video_title: Nvidia, Memory & the Next Phase of the AI Trade | Protect the Pile Episode 29
gist: Hedgeye tech analyst Felix Wang tells RPK that AI demand is flattening as token prices collapse, lab IPO and financing doubts and Rubin delays loom, memory margins face Chinese supply (CXMT, YMTC) and customer pushback, and levered neoclouds like CoreWeave are most exposed in a downturn.

insights.claim: Felix Wang says the key indicator for the AI trade into 2027 is hyperscaler plus model-lab capex, and that his own focus is enterprise spend on LLMs, which is rising only slightly month over month across the roughly 1,000 labs in his database.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: If aggregate spend is not rising in multiples, token-volume growth overstates AI revenue momentum.

insights.claim: Token volumes growing 30-40% a month are offset by token prices down 30-90% over about six months, so overall LLM spend is not compounding; Felix argues demand, not only supply, is now inflecting lower, citing Anthropic missing Q3 and OpenAI ARR not accelerating.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Price deflation undermines the volume-driven bull narrative and is a reason Hedgeye turned defensive.

insights.claim: Only about 1% of enterprises account for 80-85% of OpenAI and Anthropic spend, per research Felix cites, making AI lab revenue highly concentrated in large customers.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Concentration raises lab revenue sensitivity to a few buyers throttling spend.

insights.claim: Felix argues the AI cycle is in the mid innings rather than early: three years in, over 1,000 models, top models bunched within a couple of points of capability (excluding Mythos), and a price war is underway as models commoditize.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Commoditization favors cheap, efficient models and pressures frontier-lab pricing power.
insights.quote: we're kind of in the mid mid innings innings of AI

insights.claim: Felix says Q3 saw a large step-up in model releases and that AI helping build AI makes releases easier, so no one is following Dario's pacing argument; he sees Anthropic's paper as aimed at getting Chinese open-source models banned or restricted.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Regulatory restriction of Chinese models is the main potential brake on release cadence.

insights.claim: RPK argues that if models were frozen now, most productivity gains over the next five-plus years would come from implementation in enterprises, and Felix agrees current models are good enough for most users, which limits the economic need for further frontier gains.
insights.speaker: RPK
insights.so_what: Spend may shift from frontier training to deployment, with model fatigue slowing adoption.

themes.theme: AI lab financing, IPOs and ARR

insights.claim: Felix predicted no more large-scale IPOs this year, citing cancellations, and says Anthropic needs its IPO to restore confidence because the semiconductor complex depends on the frontier labs continuing to raise capital.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: A failed or down-priced lab IPO would hit the AI semiconductor premium.
insights.quote: there will be no more large-scale IPOs for the rest of the year

insights.claim: Private-market valuations for Anthropic of about $2 trillion or more (2.2-2.3 cited) before things rolled over would likely need a cut to about $1.5 trillion or less to list, per Felix; he says Anthropic probably missed Q3 with ARR around 70 billion, below expectations.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: A 30-50% valuation cut would reset the AI premium priced into semis.

insights.claim: RPK and Felix criticize AI labs' ARR as annualized run rate rather than true recurring revenue, with differing definitions across labs; whichever metric is used, Felix says growth is slowing.
insights.speaker: RPK and Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Benchmarking valuations on ARR overstates the revenue base.

insights.claim: RPK questions memory stocks at about five times earnings because it requires Micron-type EBITDA margins near 90% to hold for years, while China is about 30% of memory demand and CXMT is 6% of DRAM and targeting 14% within about 18 months.
insights.speaker: RPK
insights.so_what: Chinese supply growth threatens the margin durability embedded in cheap-looking multiples.

insights.claim: Felix says Nvidia, previously indifferent to memory costs, now cares because pressure reached Jensen, and optimization work led by DeepSeek aims to reduce HBM stacking and packaging needs; he would not bet on the big three (Micron, Hynix, Samsung) breaking the memory wall in their favor.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Customer pushback and architecture changes reduce memory pricing power.
insights.quote: I am not going to bet on the big three

insights.claim: Felix argues one should get around the memory wall rather than solve it, for example by using more GPUs, ASICs and networking for bandwidth, since networking is currently cheaper than memory.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Substitution toward networking and compute can erode HBM share.

insights.claim: Felix says non-AI consumer memory demand is falling off a cliff and Taiwanese PC makers are saying the memory cycle will end.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Non-AI memory weakness weakens the broad supercycle argument.

insights.claim: Felix says CXMT and YMTC are on par or better than the memory cartel in some applications, unconstrained by supply discipline mandates and backed by state support and IPOs, so he has high conviction they will gain share quickly.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: The assumption that Chinese entrants flood with low-quality product is wrong in memory, raising share-loss risk for incumbents.

insights.claim: RPK notes that no process commodity industry the Chinese entered has kept its economics, and that selling at ten when a rival's cost is two invites uneconomic competition; Felix adds that at 3-5x PE the market is pricing 85-90% margins that only the makers want, so customers regain leverage when AI slows.
insights.speaker: RPK and Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Margin normalization is the central risk to memory earnings.

insights.claim: Felix removed Nvidia from the long book after four supply-chain sources indicated Vera Rubin timing may be modified by one to two quarters due to hyperscaler specifications and new cooling and power integration; he calls it a supply-chain issue, not demand, and expects a buy-side surprise.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Delayed Rubin revenue recognition could miss buy-side expectations.

insights.claim: Felix says Nvidia's stated 0% China contribution to data center revenue is likely higher in practice, since revenue can be recognized via offshore channels or clouds, and more headlines about smuggled Blackwell chips make him antsy.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Geopolitics and China exposure remain an underappreciated Nvidia risk.

insights.claim: Felix notes Hedgeye has an 11-factor regression model for Nvidia that has nailed recent prints.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Hedgeye's quantitative Nvidia model is being used to size positions.

insights.claim: Jensen said at GTC Europe that neocloud demand is hot but access to working capital is a problem, which Felix reads as confirming financing constraints; CoreWeave is talking to insurance companies, and Nvidia, Broadcom and AMD are backing loans to AI startups, which is fine until rates rise.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Vendor financing links chip suppliers to neocloud credit risk.

insights.claim: CoreWeave is not forecast by consensus to be profitable until well into 2028; Felix says neoclouds, with five-year contracts earning mostly in the last year, are the first to blow up in an AI downturn because of leverage, and calls them very distressed for appropriate reasons.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Neoclouds are the highest-beta way to express an AI slowdown.

insights.claim: Neocloud backlog is concentrated in about five customers, the hyperscalers plus OpenAI and some Anthropic, and Felix says hyperscalers' legal teams can exit or shrink contracts if neoclouds fail to deliver equipment, so neoclouds have little leverage.
insights.speaker: Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Execution slippage gives customers outs from multi-billion backlog.

insights.claim: RPK argues hyperscalers may use neoclouds as stopgap capacity and back out once their own capacity is online, and Felix notes neoclouds compete with hyperscalers and have already pushed down H100 rental rates.
insights.speaker: RPK and Felix Wang
insights.so_what: If capex growth flattens near 1.3-1.5 trillion, hyperscalers have less reason to rent from neoclouds.

insights.claim: On October 23, 2026, the S&P 500 was about 7,624, about 2.5% below its high, with small caps down almost 10%, BB spreads at 340 bps, CCC at 1,100 bps (about 16% yield), and the 10-year just under 5%.
insights.speaker: RPK
insights.so_what: Narrow breadth and widening credit spreads contrast with a near-high index.

insights.claim: Felix notes the semiconductor ETF is still up about 30% year to date, and RPK says momentum is a factor, not a sector, so with 12-month-minus-1-month definitions tech's big lead means momentum can keep crashing as it rolls off slowly.
insights.speaker: RPK and Felix Wang
insights.so_what: Momentum factor exposure is dangerous while tech leadership unwinds.
